title: "Colors & Palettes"
author:

  - "**[Contributors]** Claude Code — AI-generated, independently AI-reviewed;"
---

Color is the most-used — and most-abused — encoding channel in scientific figures. This guide is a complete, self-contained course in three parts: **Part I** teaches the vocabulary (what a color is, the three jobs a palette can do); **Part II** goes into the science (perception, accessibility, failure modes) and surveys the R/Python ecosystem package by package; **Part III** applies everything to the scenarios you actually meet — grouped comparisons, heatmaps, survival curves, genomic tracks, and the extreme case of single-cell data with dozens to hundreds of categories. Every figure is generated by the code shown, and every palette is expressed as hex codes — the portable currency that works identically in R, Python, Illustrator and a journal's production system.

::: callout-note
**How to read this page.** If you are in a hurry: read Part I, then the checklist at the end. If you are designing a new figure standard for a lab or a paper: read Part II carefully, then follow the workflow diagram in Part III.
:::

## Setup

-   System Requirements: Cross-platform (Linux/MacOS/Windows)

-   Programming Language: R (Python equivalents are shown in Part II)

-   Dependencies: `tidyverse`; `colorspace`; `RColorBrewer`; `viridisLite`; `scico`; `pals`; `paletteer`; `dichromat`; `ggsci`; `patchwork`

```{r packages setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, output=FALSE}
# Installing necessary packages
pkgs <- c("tidyverse", "colorspace", "RColorBrewer", "viridisLite",
          "scico", "pals", "paletteer", "dichromat", "ggsci", "patchwork")
for (pkg in pkgs) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) install.packages(pkg)
}

# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(colorspace)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(viridisLite)
library(ggsci)
library(patchwork)
```

# Part I · Getting started

## Data Preparation · Part I — colors are data

On screen every color is a triple of channel intensities — red, green and blue, each 0–255 — written as a six-digit hex string. `#3A86FF` means R = 58, G = 134, B = 255. Hex codes are the lingua franca: R, Python, Inkscape, Illustrator and every journal's figure checker understand the same strings.

```{r}
#| label: pal-hex
#| fig-cap: "Anatomy of a hex color: #RRGGBB decomposes into three 0-255 channels."
#| out.width: "85%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2

hex <- "#3A86FF"
channels <- strtoi(substring(hex, c(2, 4, 6), c(3, 5, 7)), 16)

tibble(channel = c("R (red)", "G (green)", "B (blue)"), value = channels, x = 1:3,
       color = c("#E63946", "#2A9D8F", "#3A86FF")) |>
  ggplot() +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 3.4, label = hex, size = 9, family = "mono", fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 2.85, label = "= #RRGGBB  (0-255 per channel)", size = 3.6, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_col(aes(x = x, y = value, fill = color), width = .62) +
  geom_text(aes(x = x, y = value + 12, label = value), fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3, labels = c("R (red)", "G (green)", "B (blue)"), limits = c(.4, 3.6)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 4.1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "channel value (0-255)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

RGB is a *device* description, not a *perceptual* one: equal steps in RGB are not equal steps in perceived color. That mismatch is the root cause of most bad palettes — and the reason modern palettes are designed in perceptual spaces (HCL/CIELAB, and more recently OKLab), which Part II develops.

## Example · Part I — three jobs, three palette types

A palette answers exactly one of three questions. Deciding **which** is the first fork in every design:

| Job | Type | Encodes | Typical examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Distinguish categories | **Qualitative** | unordered labels | clusters, treatments, tissues |
| Show magnitude | **Sequential** | ordered low to high | expression, density, -log10(P) |
| Show deviation | **Diverging** | signed value around a centre | z-scores, log fold changes, correlations |

```{r}
#| label: pal-types
#| fig-cap: "The three palette jobs: qualitative (Set3), diverging (RdBu) and sequential (viridis)."
#| out.width: "95%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.4

strip <- function(colors, label) tibble(col = colors, x = seq_along(colors), pal = label)
bind_rows(
  strip(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(12, "Set3"), "Qualitative - ColorBrewer Set3 (12)"),
  strip(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(11, "RdBu"),  "Diverging - ColorBrewer RdBu (11)"),
  strip(viridisLite::viridis(9),               "Sequential - viridis (9)")
) |>
  mutate(pal = factor(pal, levels = c("Qualitative - ColorBrewer Set3 (12)",
                                      "Diverging - ColorBrewer RdBu (11)",
                                      "Sequential - viridis (9)"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, 1, fill = col)) +
  geom_tile(width = 1, height = .82, colour = "white", linewidth = .3) +
  facet_wrap(~pal, ncol = 1, strip.position = "left") +
  scale_fill_identity() + scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.title = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0, size = 9.5),
        strip.background = element_blank(), panel.spacing.y = unit(4, "mm"))
```

The decision tree below is the entire taxonomy on one page; Part II explains *why* each branch exists, and Part III walks through each scenario.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[What does the color encode?] --> B{Unordered categories?}
    B -- yes --> C{How many groups?}
    C -- "<= 12" --> D["Vetted qualitative set<br/>Okabe-Ito / Set2 / Set3 / ggsci"]
    C -- "13-50" --> E["Luminance tiers<br/>10 hues x 5 lightness"]
    C -- "> 50 or focus needed" --> F["Highlight: colour the few,<br/>grey the rest; facet for the rest"]
    B -- no --> G{Signed around a<br/>meaningful centre?}
    G -- yes --> H["Diverging ramp,<br/>symmetric limits at the centre"]
    G -- no --> I["Sequential ramp:<br/>viridis / cividis / scico"]
    D --> J[Check: colorblind simulation + greyscale]
    E --> J
    F --> J
    H --> J
    I --> J
    J --> K[Apply consistently; export hex codes]
```

### Your first palette in three lines

A minimal but *correct* pair of figures — one qualitative, one sequential — using the same data. The moment you set `fill`, you are choosing a palette type; here the choice is explicit:

```{r}
#| label: pal-quickstart
#| fig-cap: "Quick start: the same data with a qualitative fill (left) and a sequential fill (right)."
#| out.width: "95%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8

set.seed(7)
quick <- tibble(group = rep(c("A", "B", "C", "D"), each = 20),
                value = c(rnorm(20, 5, 1), rnorm(20, 6.5, 1.2),
                          rnorm(20, 4.4, .8), rnorm(20, 7, 1.1)))
p_q1 <- ggplot(quick, aes(group, value, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "categorical: fill = group", x = NULL, y = "value") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid = element_blank())
p_q2 <- ggplot(quick, aes(group, value, fill = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "continuous: fill = value", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
p_q1 + p_q2
```

# Part II · Going deeper

## Going deeper · Part II — perception: HCL and OKLab

Palettes should vary **hue** (which color) and **luminance** (how light) in perceptual spaces, not in RGB:

- **Sequential ramps must be luminance-monotone** — every step visibly lighter or darker than the last, so values survive greyscale printing and colorblind readers. `viridis`, `scico` and `colorspace::sequential_hcl()` are designed this way; RGB gradients are not.
- **Qualitative palettes should keep roughly constant luminance** — equal visual weight — unless you deliberately add luminance tiers to multiply the number of distinguishable colors.

R's HCL tools make the geometry explicit: `hcl()` builds a color from Hue (0–360°), Chroma (colorfulness) and Luminance (0–100); `colorspace::qualitative_hcl()`, `sequential_hcl()` and `diverging_hcl()` generate whole families within these constraints. The wheel below is that space: hue runs around the circle, luminance across the three rings — and the *top* of a sequential ramp should always travel radially, never around.

```{r}
#| label: pal-wheel
#| fig-cap: "The HCL color wheel: hue angle around the circle, three luminance rings."
#| out.width: "55%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 5.8
#| fig-height: 5.4

expand.grid(hue = 1:36, ring = 1:3) |>
  mutate(angle = (hue - .5) * 10,
         col = hcl(h = (hue - .5) * 10, c = 70, l = c(75, 60, 45)[ring]),
         r = c(.58, .79, 1)[ring],
         x = r * cos(angle * pi / 180), y = r * sin(angle * pi / 180)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x, y, colour = col), size = 6.5) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = "HCL\nwheel", fontface = "bold", size = 5, colour = "grey30") +
  coord_fixed() + labs(title = "hue angle (H) around the wheel; luminance (L) across rings") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(), axis.title = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank())
```

OKLab/OKLCH (CSS Color 4) is the newer, even more uniform space; `farver::convert_colour()` converts between representations when you need to compute rather than eyeball.

## Going deeper · Part II — accessibility: color-vision deficiency

About 8% of men of Northern European descent have a red–green color-vision deficiency (deuteranopia/protanopia); tritanopia (blue–yellow) is far rarer, and women are affected roughly an order of magnitude less often (Wong 2011). Three rules follow:

1. **Never encode a distinction in red vs green alone.** Prefer the 8-color Okabe–Ito palette, or luminance-separated palettes.
2. **Add redundant encoding** — shape, line type, direct labels — once the group count exceeds ~5.
3. **Check with a simulator.** `colorspace::deutan()` / `protan()` / `tritan()` transform hex colors, so you can render your own figure as a colorblind reader sees it.

```{r}
#| label: pal-cvd
#| fig-cap: "The Okabe-Ito palette under normal vision, deuteranopia and protanopia (colorspace::deutan/protan)."
#| out.width: "100%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.6

okabe <- c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442",
           "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#999999")
mk_panel <- function(cols, title) {
  tibble(x = 1:8, y = c(3, 5, 4, 7, 6, 8, 5.5, 4.5), g = factor(1:8), col = cols) |>
    ggplot(aes(x, y, colour = g)) +
    geom_point(size = 5) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = x, yend = y - .8), linewidth = .8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = cols) + labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank())
}
(mk_panel(okabe, "normal vision") +
   mk_panel(colorspace::deutan(okabe), "deuteranopia (red-green)") +
   mk_panel(colorspace::protan(okabe), "protanopia (red-green)")) * plot_layout(ncol = 3)
```

## Going deeper · Part II — the rainbow is (still) harmful

The rainbow spectrum is the default of many legacy tools and the most common bad choice in science. It is not perceptually uniform: it introduces **artificial band boundaries** where the data are smooth, has non-monotone luminance, and creates false landmarks. Crameri, Shephard & Heron (2020) document how such maps mislead readers. For continuous data use a perceptually uniform, colorblind-safe ramp — `viridis` (the R/Python default), `cividis` (optimized for color-vision deficiency; Nuñez et al. 2018), `scico` (the Crameri maps), or `colorspace::sequential_hcl()`.

```{r}
#| label: pal-rainbow
#| fig-cap: "The same smooth field with viridis (left) and a rainbow ramp (right) — the rainbow invents band boundaries that do not exist."
#| out.width: "100%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2

field <- expand.grid(x = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 120), y = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 120)) |>
  mutate(z = exp(-(x^2 + y^2)) + 0.5 * exp(-((x - 1.6)^2 + (y + 1.2)^2) / .6))
base_map <- function() {
  ggplot(field, aes(x, y, fill = z)) + geom_raster() +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
          panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.title = element_blank())
}
(base_map() + scale_fill_viridis_c() + labs(title = "viridis (perceptually uniform)") +
   base_map() + scale_fill_gradientn(colours = rainbow(30)) + labs(title = "rainbow (artificial bands)")) *
  plot_layout(ncol = 2)
```

## Going deeper · Part II — the ecosystem, surveyed

R has more color-palette packages than any other language; this table is the map. The *Executed here* column marks what this page demonstrates live (all such packages are pinned in the repository lockfile):

| Package | What it adds | Executed here |
|---|---|---|
| `grDevices` (base) | `hcl.colors()`, `hcl()`, `colorRampPalette()` | yes (wheel) |
| `RColorBrewer` | ColorBrewer's 35 classic schemes | yes |
| `scales` | `hue_pal()`, `gradient_n_pal()`, `show_col()` | implied |
| `colorspace` | HCL palette families + `deutan()/protan()` simulation | yes |
| `viridisLite` / `viridis` | perceptually uniform ramps (viridis, cividis, magma, ...) | yes |
| `scico` | Crameri's scientific colour maps as ggplot2/scales functions | yes |
| `ggsci` | journal palettes (Nature, Lancet, JAMA, NEJM, JCO, ...) | yes |
| `pals` | 100+ curated palettes incl. Kovesi's CET maps | yes |
| `paletteer` | a meta-package: one accessor for 100+ packages' palettes | yes |
| `dichromat` | color-vision-deficiency transformations and `dichromat()` | yes |
| `Polychrome` | `createPalette()`: dozens to hundreds of distinct colors | no |
| `cols4all` | the systematic option: 689 palettes scored for CVD-safety, fairness, nameability and contrast, with cyclic and bivariate types | no |
| `colorblindcheck` | quantitative CVD-distance checks for any palette | no |

### The measured ceilings

Two numbers worth internalizing. `RColorBrewer`'s qualitative families stop at **12 colors** — beyond that, reliable hue discrimination simply is not available. `cols4all` then turns this into a routine: every palette in its catalog carries scores for colorblind-friendliness, fairness ("do colors stand out equally?"), nameability and contrast, so palette choice becomes a query rather than a guess.

```{r}
#| label: pal-brewer
#| fig-cap: "Maximum palette size per ColorBrewer family — qualitative schemes stop at 12 colors."
#| out.width: "80%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4

RColorBrewer::brewer.pal.info |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("palette") |>
  count(category, maxcolors) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(maxcolors), n, fill = category)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", colour = "grey20", linewidth = .3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), position = position_dodge(width = .9), vjust = -.4, size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(div = "#7B3294", qual = "#008837", seq = "#2C7BB6"),
                    labels = c("diverging", "qualitative", "sequential"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "maximum colors in a ColorBrewer palette", y = "number of palettes") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .12))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

```{.r}
# cols4all — the systematic option (install.packages("cols4all")):
library(cols4all)
c4a("brewer.set2", 8)                 # exact hex colors from the 689-palette catalog
c4a_palettes(type = "div") |> head()  # browse by type: cat / seq / div / cyc / biv*
c4a_plot("brewer.set2")               # palette overview figure
c4a_scores(palette = "brewer.set2")   # quality scores: cbfriendly, fairness, nameability, contrast

# colorblindcheck — quantitative CVD distance check (install.packages("colorblindcheck")):
colorblindcheck::palette_check(c(okabe), plot = FALSE)$min_dist
```

The canonical citation for the scoring idea is the Polychrome paper for high-count palettes and the cols4all package itself (see References); the broader scientific arguments are Zeileis et al. (2009) for statistical palettes and Crameri et al. (2020) for colormaps.

### Living examples across packages

```{r}
#| label: pal-pkgmix
#| fig-cap: "Palettes accessed through four different packages: paletteer, pals, dichromat and ggsci."
#| out.width: "95%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2

pkg_rows <- list(
  "paletteer: RColorBrewer::Set2 (8)"    = paletteer::paletteer_d("RColorBrewer::Set2") |> as.character() |> (\(x) x[1:8])(),
  "pals: cols25 (10)"                    = pals::cols25(10),
  "dichromat: Okabe-Ito under deutan"    = dichromat::dichromat(okabe[1:7], "deutan"),
  "ggsci: Nature npg (10)"               = ggsci::pal_npg("nrc")(10))
purrr::imap_dfr(pkg_rows, ~ tibble(col = .x, x = seq_along(.x), pal = .y)) |>
  mutate(pal = factor(pal, levels = names(pkg_rows))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, 1, fill = col)) +
  geom_tile(width = 1, height = .8, colour = "white", linewidth = .3) +
  facet_wrap(~pal, ncol = 1, strip.position = "left") +
  scale_fill_identity() + scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.title = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0, size = 9),
        strip.background = element_blank(), panel.spacing.y = unit(3, "mm"))
```

### The Python side

The same principles and mostly the same palettes exist in Python; hex codes are portable, so a palette chosen in R works unchanged in matplotlib:

```{.python}
import matplotlib as mpl
import seaborn as sns

sns.color_palette("colorblind", 8)      # Okabe-Ito, CVD-safe categorical
mpl.colormaps["viridis"]                 # perceptually uniform sequential
mpl.colormaps["cividis"]                 # CVD-optimized sequential
sns.color_palette("deep")                # seaborn qualitative
# colorcet / cmasher / palettable additionally ship hundreds of scientific maps
# every matplotlib/seaborn palette can be dumped as hex: mpl.colors.to_hex(rgb)
```

# Part III · Applications

## Visualization · Part III — the workflow

Every figure palette goes through the same six steps; skipping the checks (3 and 4) is what produces the figures criticized in Crameri et al. (2020).

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Data + question] --> B[Pick palette type<br/>qual / seq / div]
    B --> C[Construct in a perceptual space<br/>HCL / OKLab or a vetted library]
    C --> D[Check: CVD simulation<br/>+ greyscale + print]
    D --> E[Apply consistently<br/>one palette per figure family]
    E --> F[Export hex codes<br/>into the methods/legend]
    D -- fails --> B
```

## Visualization · Part III — grouped comparisons

The classic bar/box/violin comparison with 2–6 groups: a journal qualitative palette, constant luminance, and enough redundancy (direct labels, shapes) that the figure survives color-vision deficiency. Four groups is comfortably inside the reliable range.

```{r}
#| label: pal-grouped
#| fig-cap: "Grouped comparison with a journal palette (ggsci npg): violin + box overlay."
#| out.width: "75%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 4.2

set.seed(11)
groups <- tibble(
  group = factor(rep(c("Control", "Low dose", "High dose", "Combo"), each = 24),
                 levels = c("Control", "Low dose", "High dose", "Combo")),
  value = c(rnorm(24, 4, 1), rnorm(24, 5, 1.1), rnorm(24, 6.2, 1.2), rnorm(24, 7.4, 1.3)))
ggplot(groups, aes(group, value, fill = group)) +
  geom_violin(width = .75, colour = NA, alpha = .85, scale = "width") +
  geom_boxplot(width = .12, fill = "white", outlier.shape = NA, linewidth = .35) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal_npg("nrc")(4)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Response score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10))
```

## Visualization · Part III — heatmaps and matrices

For a heatmap the palette follows the data, not the package: unsigned magnitudes get a sequential ramp; signed values get a diverging ramp **centred and symmetric at zero** — otherwise the neutral color sits off-centre and readers misread the sign structure. With `ComplexHeatmap`, anchor the scale at meaningful values: `colorRamp2(c(0, 5, 10), viridis(3))`.

```{r}
#| label: pal-heat
#| fig-cap: "Two heatmap palettes: signed z-scores (diverging, symmetric at 0) and unsigned magnitude (sequential)."
#| out.width: "100%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2

set.seed(3)
mat <- matrix(rnorm(120), 12, 10, dimnames = list(paste0("G", 1:12), paste0("S", 1:10)))
hm_panel <- function(m, title, fill) {
  as_tibble(m, rownames = "gene") |>
    pivot_longer(-gene) |>
    ggplot(aes(name, gene, fill = value)) + geom_tile() +
    scale_fill_gradientn(colours = fill, limits = c(-2.6, 2.6), oob = scales::squish) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8),
          axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8), panel.grid = element_blank())
}
hm_panel(mat, "z-score: diverging, symmetric at 0", rev(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(11, "RdBu"))) +
  hm_panel(abs(mat), "magnitude: sequential (viridis)", viridis(11))
```

## Visualization · Part III — survival and clinical curves

Clinical curves usually carry 2–4 groups, where the Okabe-Ito colors plus direct labels (not a legend far away) are ideal. Keep one palette across all clinical panels of the paper — a consistency requirement, not a style preference.

```{r}
#| label: pal-km
#| fig-cap: "Simulated Kaplan-Meier curves: three groups in Okabe-Ito colors with an embedded legend."
#| out.width: "70%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.2

set.seed(5)
grid <- seq(0, 24, by = 1)
km <- purrr::map_dfr(1:3, function(g) {
  rate <- c(.09, .05, .028)[g]
  surv <- cumprod(c(1, exp(-rate * diff(grid) * rnorm(length(grid) - 1, 1, .15))))
  tibble(time = grid, surv = surv,
         group = factor(c("Low risk", "Intermediate", "High risk")[g],
                        levels = c("Low risk", "Intermediate", "High risk")))
})
ggplot(km, aes(time, surv, colour = group)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = .9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Low risk" = "#0072B2",
                                 "Intermediate" = "#E69F00",
                                 "High risk" = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Months", y = "Overall survival", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = c(.75, .8), legend.background = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

## Visualization · Part III — genomic tracks and enrichment figures

Genomics has its own conventions: the **chromosome palette** below is the widely used 24-color scheme (each chromosome gets a stable color; adjacent chromosomes differ in hue *and* family), and mutation-type legends follow the same logic at 5–10 categories. Enrichment bar/dot plots are a hybrid: a sequential scale carries significance (`-log10(P)`) while categories stay near-neutral — tempting to rainbow, but the sequential rule wins.

```{r}
#| label: pal-chrom
#| fig-cap: "The conventional 24-color chromosome palette applied to a schematic gene-count track."
#| out.width: "95%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 3.6

chrom_cols <- c(rep("#8DD3C7", 3), rep("#BEBADA", 3), rep("#FB8072", 3),
                rep("#80B1D3", 3), rep("#FDB462", 3), rep("#B3DE69", 3),
                rep("#FCCDE5", 3), rep("#D9D9D9", 2), "#BC80BD")
chrom <- tibble(
  chr = factor(paste0("chr", c(1:22, "X", "Y")), levels = paste0("chr", c(1:22, "X", "Y"))),
  col = chrom_cols,
  n = c(249, 243, 198, 191, 181, 171, 159, 146, 141, 135, 135, 134,
        115, 107, 102, 90, 83, 80, 59, 64, 47, 51, 156, 57))
ggplot(chrom, aes(chr, n, fill = col)) +
  geom_col(width = .8) + scale_fill_identity() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Genes (schematic)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

## Visualization · Part III — the extreme case: many categories

A scRNA-seq UMAP routinely has 20–50 clusters — the hardest case for color. ggplot2's default discrete scale generates one hue per level, so 50 classes land ~7° apart on the hue wheel: all distinct hex codes, perceptually one continuous blur.

```{r}
#| label: pal-50-clusters
#| fig-cap: "50 simulated clusters: the ggplot default hue palette (left) vs 10 hues x 5 luminance tiers (right)."
#| out.width: "100%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

set.seed(2026)
n_cl <- 50
centres <- tibble(cl = 1:n_cl,
                  cx = cos(seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n_cl)) * 10 + rnorm(n_cl, 0, 1.2),
                  cy = sin(seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n_cl)) * 10 + rnorm(n_cl, 0, 1.2))
embed <- purrr::map_dfr(1:n_cl, function(i) {
  tibble(cl = i, x = rnorm(45, centres$cx[i], .55), y = rnorm(45, centres$cy[i], .55))
}) |> mutate(cl = factor(sprintf("C%02d", cl)))

pal50 <- hcl(h = rep(seq(15, 375, length.out = 10), times = 5),
             c = rep(c(75, 85, 75, 65, 55), each = 10),
             l = rep(c(78, 68, 58, 48, 38), each = 10))
names(pal50) <- levels(embed$cl)

map_base <- function() {
  ggplot(embed, aes(x, y, colour = cl)) + geom_point(size = .55, alpha = .9) +
    coord_fixed() + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
          legend.position = "none", axis.title = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
}
(map_base() + labs(title = "ggplot default hue palette (50 classes)") +
   map_base() + scale_colour_manual(values = pal50) +
   labs(title = "10 hues x 5 luminance tiers")) * plot_layout(ncol = 2)
```

Even a well-built 50-color palette is at the edge of human discrimination. The published strategies, in order of reliability:

1. **Highlight** — colour the clusters you discuss, grey the rest. This is what real papers do beyond ~15 groups.
2. **Luminance tiers** — 10 hues × 5 lightness levels is a practical ceiling; reuse the *same* palette across every plot (`DimPlot(cols = ...)` / `scale_colour_manual(values = ...)`).
3. **Split** — facet the UMAP by condition (or Seurat's `split.by`) so each panel carries ~10 categories.
4. **Programmatic generation** — `Polychrome::createPalette()` optimizes hue, chroma and luminance jointly for hundreds of colors.

```{r}
#| label: pal-highlight
#| fig-cap: "The highlighting strategy: focal clusters coloured, everything else grey."
#| out.width: "65%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 5.6

focal <- c("C07", "C23", "C41")
embed |>
  mutate(col = if_else(cl %in% focal, as.character(cl), "other")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, colour = col)) +
  geom_point(size = .55, alpha = .9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(set_names(c("#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#009E73"), focal),
                                 other = "grey85"),
                      breaks = focal) +
  coord_fixed() + labs(colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.title = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Visualization · Part III — one palette everywhere

The final discipline: a paper is a *system*, not a collection of figures. Define one palette per meaning, reuse it across every panel and every figure type, and document the hex codes. The triptych below uses the same four colors for the same four groups in a box plot, a line chart and a bar chart.

```{r}
#| label: pal-consistency
#| fig-cap: "One palette, three chart types: consistency is a scientific requirement, not a style preference."
#| out.width: "95%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4

set.seed(9)
cons_cols <- c(A = "#4C78A8", B = "#F58518", C = "#54A24B", D = "#B279A2")
cons <- tibble(g = factor(rep(names(cons_cols), each = 10), levels = names(cons_cols)),
               v = rnorm(40, 5, 1.2), t = rep(1:10, 4))
c1 <- ggplot(cons, aes(g, v, fill = g)) + geom_boxplot(width = .55, outlier.shape = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cons_cols) + labs(title = "box", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
c2 <- ggplot(cons, aes(t, v, colour = g, group = g)) + geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cons_cols) + labs(title = "line", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
c3 <- ggplot(cons |> count(g), aes(g, n, fill = g)) + geom_col(width = .6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cons_cols) + labs(title = "bar", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
c1 + c2 + c3
```

## Rules of thumb

::: callout-tip
**A checklist for every figure**

1. **Match the palette type to the job**: qualitative ≠ sequential ≠ diverging.
2. **Continuous values get luminance-monotone ramps**; never the rainbow.
3. **Signed data gets a diverging scale centred and symmetric at zero.**
4. **Categorical data**: ≤ 12 colors from a vetted set (Set2/Set3, Okabe-Ito, ggsci); beyond that use luminance tiers, redundant encodings, highlighting or facets.
5. **Check colorblind readability** (`colorspace::deutan()`, `colorblindcheck::palette_check()`); prefer Okabe-Ito / viridis / cividis / scico.
6. **One palette per meaning, everywhere** in the paper; document the hex codes.
7. **Never rely on color alone** for a categorical decision.
8. **Print check**: convert to greyscale once — if two groups merge, the palette failed.
:::
